summary: This experimental document introduces FCAST, an application for reliably delivering objects such as files. It runs on top of either the ALC/LCT reliable multicast transport protocol or the NORM transport protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a way to send the same file to many computers at once, repeating until everyone has it.

questions: reliable multicast file delivery alc norm
how does carousel instance descriptor work
subtitle: Reliably delivering files to many receivers at once using multicast protocols

tldr.problem: Broadcasting the same file to hundreds or thousands of receivers using traditional unicast TCP requires proportional bandwidth from the sender, and unreliable multicast leaves no way to ensure everyone receives the complete file.
tldr.mechanism: FCAST wraps files in a compound object with metadata, sends them over either the ALC (Asynchronous Layered Coding) or NORM (NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast) transport protocols, and manages a carousel of objects that repeats until all receivers have obtained them.
tldr.outcome: Bandwidth-efficient, scalable file distribution to many receivers with delivery guarantees adapted to the protocol choice, ranging from fully reliable with feedback to best-effort with repetition.

today: RFC 6968 is an Experimental protocol for reliable file delivery over multicast. It has not been obsoleted and remains the basis for implementations of FCAST/ALC and FCAST/NORM file distribution systems.

sections.title: Overview and Design Goals
sections.content:
FCAST is a reliable object delivery application designed to send files to groups of receivers efficiently. It runs on top of either ALC (Asynchronous Layered Coding with the LCT transport) or NORM (NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast), both of which offer multicast delivery.

Unlike traditional unicast where a separate connection streams each file to each receiver, FCAST sends all receivers the same data simultaneously. Receivers that need repairs can request missing pieces, or if using ALC, they simply receive the carousel again until they have the whole file.

The design favors simplicity over flexibility. Metadata (file names, sizes, types) is bundled with each file in a Compound Object rather than sent separately. This ensures receivers always have the metadata they need, but means they cannot pre-filter files before starting to download them. The protocol defines required and optional features to keep implementations lightweight.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a radio station broadcasting the same song over and over. Listeners tune in whenever and download as many repetitions as they need until they have the whole thing.

sections.title: Core Concepts: Compound Objects and the Carousel
sections.content:
A Compound Object is an FCAST Header (containing metadata) followed by the actual file data. The header is 8 bytes minimum and uses fields to specify the format and encoding of metadata (such as HTTP headers) and a checksum to detect corruption.

The Carousel is a cycle of repeated transmission. During each cycle, all registered files are sent one or more times. When files are added or removed, a new Carousel Instance is defined. The sender creates a Carousel Instance Descriptor (CID), a special object listing which file identifiers belong to the current instance. The CID can announce when the session is complete, helping receivers know when they can leave.

Files are identified by a Transport Object Identifier (TOI) assigned by the underlying protocol. In NORM, TOIs must increase monotonically, so if an old file needs to be resent in a new carousel, it gets a new TOI and the CID signals that the two TOIs refer to the same object (TOI equivalence).
sections.plainLanguage: Each file comes with a label (the metadata). They are sent repeatedly in rounds called carousels. A special message lists which files are in the current round.

sections.title: Header Format and Metadata
sections.content:
The FCAST Header begins with an 8-byte fixed section containing version, reserved bits, a global checksum flag, a CID flag indicating if this is a special list object, the metadata format (e.g., HTTP/1.1), and the metadata encoding (UTF-8 or GZIP compressed UTF-8).

Metadata uses HTTP-style key-value pairs: Content-Location (file name and URI), Content-Type (MIME type), Content-Length (file size), Content-Encoding (if the file was compressed), and FCAST-specific entries like Fcast-Obj-Digest-SHA256 (a hash to verify integrity), and Fcast-Obj-Slice-* entries for very large files split into pieces.

The CID's Object List is a comma-delimited text string of TOI values, ranges (e.g., '1,2,4-6'), and TOI equivalence mappings (e.g., '(10=5/2)' means 'TOI 10 is the same object as TOI 5 from Carousel Instance 2'). This list can optionally be compressed, and is preceded by metadata entries Fcast-CID-Complete (set to 1 when no more files will arrive) and Fcast-CID-ID (numbering the carousel instance).
sections.plainLanguage: The file label contains its name, type, size, and a number to check if it got scrambled. Very big files can be split into pieces.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Behavior
sections.content:
The sender collects files and metadata, assigns a TOI to each, and registers them in the current Carousel Instance. When ready, the sender creates a CID if desired (which is optional), picks a transmission schedule, and begins the carousel. Files repeat during each cycle. The sender may transmit a new CID periodically, and if the set of files changes, a new Carousel Instance is created with a fresh CIID.

The receiver joins the session and collects packets. If an FCAST Header becomes fully available (which may happen before the entire file arrives in some ALC/NORM configurations), the receiver can read the metadata and decide whether to continue receiving the file. When a complete Compound Object arrives, the receiver verifies the metadata, optionally decompresses the file, and validates the checksum. Upon receiving a CID, the receiver notes which files are in the current instance and may discard files from previous instances that are no longer relevant. If the CID marks the session complete and the receiver has all files, it can exit the session.

FCAST/ALC provides best-effort delivery repeated over many cycles; FCAST/NORM allows receivers to request missing pieces, potentially achieving fully reliable delivery if the sender grants the repair requests. Scalability differs: ALC is massively scalable (no feedback), while NORM is limited by its feedback mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender lists files, labels them, and broadcasts them in rounds. The receiver gets packets and reads the label to decide whether to keep downloading. If a CID says no more files are coming and the receiver has them all, it can stop.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
FCAST itself does not provide encryption or authentication; it relies on the underlying ALC or NORM protocols and additional mechanisms. Attackers could send forged packets, corrupt metadata or CIDs, or tamper with transport protocol parameters.

For confidentiality and access control, the entire object or each packet should be encrypted (e.g., using IPsec/ESP). For integrity and sender authentication, several techniques are recommended: digitally sign objects or packets, use a Group-keyed MAC scheme shared among trusted group members, use TESLA (Timed Efficient Stream Loss-Tolerant Authentication, suitable for multicast), or apply IPsec/ESP.

The IANA registry defines three metadata formats and encodings and lists the standard metadata types. Developers can propose new types via Expert Review. FCAST is compatible with any congestion control, FEC scheme, or security mechanism designed for ALC or NORM, and works with both IPv4 and IPv6. The delivery service is fully reliable only if ALC or NORM repair mechanisms are enabled and the carousel runs long enough, or if a session control application extends the session until all receivers confirm receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: FCAST does not have built-in secrets; it uses encryption and signatures from other protocols. An attacker could change files during sending, so you should sign or encrypt them.

sections.title: Use Cases and Comparison to FLUTE
sections.content:
FCAST is suited to scenarios where all receivers want most or all of the files in a session (e.g., mirroring, broadcasting updates to many sites, distributing patches). In such cases, the limitation that metadata arrives with each file, not ahead of time, is not a problem.

FCAST/ALC is ideal for purely unidirectional networks (broadcast-only) or where receivers have limited bandwidth to send repair requests. FCAST/NORM suits networks where feedback channels are available and reliability is critical.

FLUTE (RFC 6726), an alternative reliable multicast file delivery protocol, favors flexibility at the cost of greater complexity. FLUTE allows metadata to be sent separately, enabling receivers to decide whether to download individual files before reception starts, a capability FCAST lacks by design. FCAST's simpler, lighter-weight approach is a deliberate trade-off.
sections.plainLanguage: FCAST works best when receivers want many files. If receivers need to pick and choose files before downloading, FLUTE is better but more complicated.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: FCAST protocol version (0 in this spec).

fields.name: Global
fields.desc: If 1, checksum covers whole object; if 0, header only.

fields.name: CID Flag
fields.desc: If 1, this is a Carousel Instance Descriptor.

fields.name: Header Length
fields.desc: Total length of FCAST header in bytes (including variable metadata).
